content.body:
## Overview

The work-planner skill lives in prosiform-skills, with its history and the shared files it is checked against, and the workspace that uses it runs it from a pinned commit of that repository. workflow-server's `workspace` template carries no copy, the skill then fits its new root, and each board's Priority field is the one source of a rank. The skill is used through prosiform: a session selects a mode from the entry point, runs `pf` on that mode and follows its bundle, every mode compiles within prosiform's default output budget with no warning and against stubs of its artifacts and protocols, a link stands only where its reader must have the content and names the section it needs, and the shared guide and check state, define and enforce those rules. The goal the reviews test against is one home for the skill, cut over and linked before any refactoring, ranking work by the board and used through prosiform.

## Problem

The skill has no home of its own, and it is written for a reader who follows links one at a time while prosiform compiles every local link into one bundle.

- **It lives inside an unrelated repository.**
  Its [entry point](https://github.com/m2ux/workflow-server/blob/785a5ee8c715b802498aa41712e0489425a22cfa/skills/work-planner/SKILL.md#L1-L5) sits in workflow-server's `skills/` beside three other skills, so its history and pull requests are workflow-server's.
- **Its install is a copy.**
  prosiform's workspace receives the skill as plain files from workflow-server's template, and records no version.
- **Its commands assume that layout.**
  71 occurrences of `skills/work-planner` in 22 of its files hold only under a `skills/` folder.
- **A rank has two homes.**
  Board Queue ranks by [`priority:` labels](https://github.com/m2ux/workflow-server/blob/785a5ee8c715b802498aa41712e0489425a22cfa/skills/work-planner/scripts/board-queue.py#L33), while board 17's Priority field is a single-select nothing reads.
- **Five modes overflow the default budget.**
  At [785a5ee8c](https://github.com/m2ux/workflow-server/tree/785a5ee8c715b802498aa41712e0489425a22cfa/skills/work-planner), Deliver compiles to 353717 bytes, Plan 328950, Advance 314874, Standup 273929 and Sync 264276, against a default output budget of 262144.
- **A mode's prerequisites compile other modes whole.**
  [Plan Mode's Prerequisites](https://github.com/m2ux/workflow-server/blob/785a5ee8c715b802498aa41712e0489425a22cfa/skills/work-planner/modes/plan-mode.md#L11-L27) link Propose Mode and Sync Mode, so the Plan bundle carries both although its steps run each in only one case.
- **Hand-offs are prose.**
  [Deliver Mode](https://github.com/m2ux/workflow-server/blob/785a5ee8c715b802498aa41712e0489425a22cfa/skills/work-planner/modes/deliver-mode.md#L101-L105) starts a unit's session through a sentence, and no link carries a dispatch or deferral operator.
- **Links name whole files.**
  245 of the skill's 1075 internal links name a whole file whose content carries sections, and each compiles that whole file into the bundle.
- **The rules describe reading, not compiling.**
  The [shared Links rules](https://github.com/m2ux/workflow-server/blob/785a5ee8c715b802498aa41712e0489425a22cfa/skills/guidelines.md#L105-L118) type links for a reader who chooses what to open, and say nothing of a bundle, an operator or a budget.
- **Nothing compiles the skill.**
  The [shared skill-file check](https://github.com/m2ux/workflow-server/blob/785a5ee8c715b802498aa41712e0489425a22cfa/skills/scripts/check_skill_files.py#L1025-L1029) reads link resolution and placement, so a mode that overflows the budget or reaches another mode whole draws no finding.
- **A check is named by its path.**
  The shared guidelines' [Verified rule](https://github.com/m2ux/workflow-server/blob/785a5ee8c715b802498aa41712e0489425a22cfa/skills/guidelines.md#L198) names the shared check as a code span, and their [Files rule](https://github.com/m2ux/workflow-server/blob/785a5ee8c715b802498aa41712e0489425a22cfa/skills/guidelines.md#L27-L28) says where checks sit without saying what any of them decides.

## Proposal

- **Cut over first, unchanged.**
  The skill's history and the shared guide, rules, check and tests move as they are to the root of prosiform-skills, in the shape workflow-server's `skills/` folder had.
- **Planning and delivery follow the skill.**
  Task and epic pull requests target `main`, and planning records live on an orphan `engineering` branch.
- **Skills belong to each workspace.**
  The workspace that uses the skill vendors prosiform-skills as a submodule pinned to a commit and links the skill into its `skills/`. workflow-server's template supports that pattern, vendors nothing itself, and drops its copy.
- **Refactor after the link.**
  Only once the skill is linked does it change: its commands and the shared check fit the new root, and the board's Priority field replaces the priority labels.
- **The shared guide states the prosiform rules.**
  A skill bootstraps by running `pf`; a link names the section its reader must have, and a mention is plain text; `⇉` and `⫽` carry hand-offs and `¬` conditional reads; each mode fits the default budget.
- **A check is defined where prose names it.**
  The shared guide defines each check prosiform-skills runs, and prose names a check by linking to that definition.
- **The skill is brought to the rules, then held to them.**
  Its links, hand-offs, entry point and modes conform first; the shared check then enforces the prosiform rules over every skill it runs over, and each mode's bundle size is recorded against a fixed baseline revision.

## Work Breakdown

| [E00](https://github.com/m2ux/prosiform-skills/issues/2) | Skill Cutover | AC1 | | |
| [E01](https://github.com/m2ux/prosiform-skills/issues/3) | Workspace Linkage | AC3, AC4 | | |
| [E02](https://github.com/m2ux/prosiform-skills/issues/5) | Skill Refactor | AC2 | [E00](https://github.com/m2ux/prosiform-skills/issues/2), [E01](https://github.com/m2ux/prosiform-skills/issues/3) | |
| [E03](https://github.com/m2ux/prosiform-skills/issues/4) | Priority Field | AC5, AC6 | [E00](https://github.com/m2ux/prosiform-skills/issues/2), [E01](https://github.com/m2ux/prosiform-skills/issues/3) | |
| [E04](https://github.com/m2ux/prosiform-skills/issues/6) | Shared Prosiform Rules | AC12 | [E00](https://github.com/m2ux/prosiform-skills/issues/2), [E01](https://github.com/m2ux/prosiform-skills/issues/3) | |
| [E05](https://github.com/m2ux/prosiform-skills/issues/7) | Check Definitions | AC14 | [E02](https://github.com/m2ux/prosiform-skills/issues/5) |  |
| [E06](https://github.com/m2ux/prosiform-skills/issues/8) | Work Planner Links | AC9, AC10 | [E02](https://github.com/m2ux/prosiform-skills/issues/5), [E04](https://github.com/m2ux/prosiform-skills/issues/6) | |
| [E07](https://github.com/m2ux/prosiform-skills/issues/9) | Use Through Prosiform | AC7, AC8, AC9, AC11, AC13, AC15, AC16 | [E06](https://github.com/m2ux/prosiform-skills/issues/8) | |

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] **AC1.** The work-planner skill and the shared files it is checked against stand at the root of prosiform-skills' `main` with the history they had in workflow-server, as a tree and log comparison against the extracted workflow-server commit shows.
- [ ] **AC2.** The skill's tests and the shared check pass from the root of a prosiform-skills checkout, as their runs on `main` show.
- [ ] **AC3.** workflow-server's `workspace` template carries no copy of the skill, and none of its skill files outside workflow-canon names it, as a listing and a grep of its head show.
- [ ] **AC4.** prosiform's workspace runs the skill from a prosiform-skills commit it pins, as the skill's test suite run through its link in a fresh clone shows.
- [ ] **AC5.** Board Queue ranks each theme board's work by its board item's Priority number, as the queue's tests show.
- [ ] **AC6.** No repository whose issues a theme board holds carries a `priority:` label, as a label listing of each shows.
- [ ] **AC7.** Every Work Planner mode on `main` compiles under the pinned `pf` within its default output budget with no warning, as the shared skill-file check's compile run reports over `work-planner`.
- [ ] **AC8.** A session given a Work Planner request selects a mode from the entry point, runs `pf` on that mode and follows its bundle, as a walk of a representative request from the entry point records.
- [ ] **AC9.** No Work Planner link compiles content its reader need not have, whether a whole file whose target carries sections or another mode reached outside a dispatch or a deferral, as the shared skill-file check reports over `work-planner`.
- [ ] **AC10.** Each Work Planner hand-off to a sub-agent dispatches the procedure followed, and each citation a step reads only in some cases is deferred, as the hand-off and conditional-citation inventories the planning record holds show against the compiled bundles.
- [ ] **AC11.** No Work Planner mode's compiled bundle is larger than at the baseline revision the planning record fixes, as the bundle-size comparison records using one prosiform version on both revisions.
- [ ] **AC12.** `guidelines.md` states the rules a skill used through prosiform follows — its bootstrap, its links, its operators and its budget — as a read of the guidelines on `main` shows.
- [ ] **AC13.** The shared skill-file check reports a violation of each prosiform rule it decides in any skill it runs over, as the check's own test suite shows against specimen skills.
- [ ] **AC14.** Prose in Work Planner and the shared guide reaches each check prosiform-skills runs through a definition stating what it decides, which skills it binds, how it is run and where its tests live, as the shared skill-file check reports over `work-planner`.
- [ ] **AC15.** Every Work Planner mode compiles under the pinned `pf` with its test preset, whose substitutions stand stubs in for the artifacts and protocols it links, as the skill's test suite shows.
- [ ] **AC16.** Work Planner's protocols and artifacts, and the procedures, operations, commands and fields they hold, are cut to the grain its rubric states, and Revise Mode holds each new or changed one to that rubric, as the grain report the planning record holds and a read of `work-planner/references/grain-rubric.md` on `main` show.

## Non-Goals

- It moves no skill other than work-planner.
- It keeps the two repositories' copies of the shared skill files in step by no mechanism.
- It adds no prosiform-skills submodule to workflow-server's template, so a workspace made from it receives no work-planner.
- It leaves workflow-canon's `references/revise-mode.md` naming `skills/work-planner`.
- It leaves the proposals boards' Priority field as it stands.
- It sets no Priority value beyond the one a numbered label carried.
- It changes neither prosiform nor its default budgets.
- It generates and checks no read-set manifest for any skill.
- It walks neither retrieval order nor citation efficacy, which compilation settles.

The extraction is cut from workflow-server's `workspace` head once I17's Pre-Cutover Fixes epic closes.

## Overview

This epic cuts the work-planner skill over to its own repository. The skill, with its history and the shared guide, rules, check and tests it is held to, moves from workflow-server's `skills/` folder to the root of prosiform-skills as it is, with no change to its content.

## Problem

The skill shares a repository with work it has nothing to do with.

- **It lives in workflow-server.**
  Its [entry point](https://github.com/m2ux/workflow-server/blob/785a5ee8c715b802498aa41712e0489425a22cfa/skills/work-planner/SKILL.md#L1-L5) sits beside three unrelated skills, so its history and pull requests are workflow-server's.
- **The new repository has no `main`.**
  prosiform-skills holds only its orphan `engineering` branch, which GitHub made its default branch.
- **Nothing states its branches.**
  prosiform-skills has no `config/branches`, so the skill's branch reads there report the names unevaluable.

## Proposal

- **History moves with the files.**
  `git filter-repo` keeps `skills/work-planner/`, `skills/guidelines.md`, `skills/rules.json`, `skills/scripts/check_skill_files.py` and `skills/test/test_check_skill_files.py`, and moves them up one level.
- **Content moves unchanged.**
  No file's content changes. The skill's commands still name `skills/work-planner/scripts/<name>.py`, which holds in a workspace that links the skill at `skills/work-planner`.
- **The extraction is `main`'s first history.**
  It is pushed directly, before any epic base exists, and `main` becomes the default branch. It is cut from workflow-server's `workspace` head once I17's Pre-Cutover Fixes, Skill Separation and Skill Style epics close, and its tree is compared with workflow-server's at that commit.
- **The repository states its branches.**
  `config/branches` names `main`, which task and epic pull requests target, and `engineering`, which holds planning records.

content.body:
## Overview

This epic links the work-planner skill into the workspace that uses it. prosiform's workspace takes the skill from a prosiform-skills submodule pinned to a commit, workflow-server's `workspace` template supports that vendor pattern without vendoring the skill itself, and the template's plain copy goes.

## Problem

The skill reaches its workspace as a copy, and the template's scripts know no other way.

- **A copy, not a version.**
  workflow-server's template holds [`skills/work-planner`](https://github.com/m2ux/workflow-server/tree/785a5ee8c715b802498aa41712e0489425a22cfa/skills/work-planner) as plain files. prosiform's workspace takes them through template updates, and nothing records which skill commit it runs.
- **Deploy skips submodules.**
  `deploy-workspace.sh` [clones the workspace branch](https://github.com/m2ux/workflow-server/blob/785a5ee8c715b802498aa41712e0489425a22cfa/scripts/deploy-workspace.sh#L85-L86) without its submodules.
- **Update skips submodules.**
  `update-workspace.sh` [merges the template](https://github.com/m2ux/workflow-server/blob/785a5ee8c715b802498aa41712e0489425a22cfa/scripts/update-workspace.sh#L31-L33) and leaves any submodule as it was.
- **The shared check names the copy.**
  The check's [usage](https://github.com/m2ux/workflow-server/blob/785a5ee8c715b802498aa41712e0489425a22cfa/skills/scripts/check_skill_files.py#L79-L80) and a [guide example](https://github.com/m2ux/workflow-server/blob/785a5ee8c715b802498aa41712e0489425a22cfa/skills/guidelines.md#L140) name `work-planner` under `skills/`.

## Proposal

- **Skills belong to each workspace.**
  The template declares no prosiform-skills submodule. A workspace that uses a skill from another repository vendors it under `vendor/` and links it into `skills/`.
- **The template's scripts support the vendor pattern.**
  `deploy-workspace.sh` and `update-workspace.sh` check out whatever submodules a workspace declares, at their pinned commits.
- **prosiform's workspace links the skill.**
  It first takes the template's script change, then adds prosiform-skills as a full submodule at `vendor/prosiform-skills`, with no sparse checkout, pinned to a commit on `main`. `skills/work-planner` becomes a tracked symlink to `../vendor/prosiform-skills/work-planner`, so the skill runs unchanged.
- **The template's copy goes after the link.**
  The template deletes `skills/work-planner` only once prosiform's link has merged, so prosiform never has neither copy.
- **The removal merges cleanly into prosiform.**
  At prosiform's next template update, both sides have deleted the plain files and only prosiform's side holds the symlink, so the merge keeps the symlink with no conflict.
- **workflow-canon is left as it stands.**
  Its `references/revise-mode.md` still names `skills/work-planner`.

## Work Breakdown

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [W01](https://github.com/m2ux/prosiform-skills/blob/engineering/artifacts/planning/2026-11-02-1-i16-work-planner-repository/e01/w01.md) | Deploy checks out submodules | AC1 | | | | |
| [W02](https://github.com/m2ux/prosiform-skills/blob/engineering/artifacts/planning/2026-11-02-1-i16-work-planner-repository/e01/w02.md) | Update checks out submodules | AC2 | | | | |
| [W03](https://github.com/m2ux/prosiform-skills/blob/engineering/artifacts/planning/2026-11-02-1-i16-work-planner-repository/e01/w03.md) | prosiform workspace links the skill | AC3, AC4, AC5 | W01, W02, [E00:W00](https://github.com/m2ux/prosiform-skills/issues/2) | | | |
| [W04](https://github.com/m2ux/prosiform-skills/blob/engineering/artifacts/planning/2026-11-02-1-i16-work-planner-repository/e01/w04.md) | Plain copy removed from the template | AC6, AC7, AC8 | W03 | | | |

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] **AC1.** `deploy-workspace.sh` makes a workspace whose submodules stand at the commits that workspace pins, as a deploy from a fixture workspace carrying a submodule shows.
- [ ] **AC2.** `update-workspace.sh` leaves a workspace's submodules at the commits it pins after the template merges in, as an update of a fixture fork whose submodule pin moves shows.
- [ ] **AC3.** prosiform's `workspace` has a full prosiform-skills submodule at `vendor/prosiform-skills`, pinned to a commit that prosiform-skills' `main` contains, as `git submodule status` and `git branch -r --contains` of the pinned commit show.
- [ ] **AC4.** prosiform's `skills/work-planner` is a tracked symlink to `../vendor/prosiform-skills/work-planner`, as `git ls-tree` of its `workspace` shows.
- [ ] **AC5.** The skill's test suite passes run through `skills/work-planner` in a fresh clone of prosiform's `workspace` with its submodules, as `python3 -m unittest discover -s skills/work-planner/test` there shows.
- [ ] **AC6.** workflow-server's `workspace` template tracks no file under `skills/work-planner/`, as `git ls-tree -r` of its head shows.
- [ ] **AC7.** No file under the template's `skills/` outside `skills/workflow-canon` names work-planner, as `git grep -n work-planner -- skills ':!skills/workflow-canon'` shows.
- [ ] **AC8.** workflow-server's shared test suite passes on `workspace`, as `python3 -m unittest discover -s skills/test` shows.

content.body:
## Overview

Agent-engineering work in this repository is planned, tracked and delivered through one skill. A request to propose work, break it down, review a plan, bring it in step with what has landed, or hand out what is ready is served by a mode of that skill, and the issues it writes are the plan. Every initiative stands on its theme's board, every criterion states one invariant a named instrument can fail, and a board can be read as a standup or walked for the work it makes available.

## Problem

The scheme that plans every other piece of work is the one body of work with no plan.

- **Requirements held outside the plan.**
  The skill was built by directive across many pull requests. What was required of it is held in the session transcripts and the specification drawn from them, so a change to the skill is checked against an intent only where the plan answers to that specification.
- **No criteria to check against.**
  Nothing states what the skill must achieve, so a regression in one mode is caught only when someone notices the output is wrong.
- **Rules the skill states but nothing checks.**
  The conventions binding the skill's own files — its frontmatter, its command specifications, its prose layout, its vocabulary — are prose, so conformance rests on whoever remembers them.
- **Work outside any structure.**
  Issues raised against the skill sit in the tracker with no initiative above them, so they reach no board view and no dependency check.
- **A complete epic waits on a click.**
  Its review pull request stays a draft until the user marks it ready, though every condition for that mark is one the delivery scripts already establish.
- **A theme with no home.**
  The scheme is engineering process, not the definition product the existing themes describe, so its work has nowhere to stand.

## Proposal

- **One initiative over the scheme.**
  The skill's delivered work and its open work are planned as epics of a single initiative, on a board of its own theme.
- **The specification is the source.**
  The requirements drawn from the sessions in which the scheme was argued stand as one document, and the initiative's criteria answer to it in both directions.
- **Criteria over the whole scheme.**
  Each criterion states an outcome the modes achieve together, kept by the skill's fixture suite or by a check run over the repository's live issues and boards.
- **Every house rule reaches a check.**
  A rule a script can decide is reached through a named operation, the skill's own files included, so conformance is measurable across the tracker and across the skill at once.
- **Delivery settles what the board and the review show.**
  A completed epic's review pull request stands for user review once completion checks and agent review of its current integration head and base pass without blocking findings; delivery statuses account for reservations and open work.
- **The open work joins the structure.**
  Issues raised against the skill become tasks of an epic, or take the standalone layout where no goal covers them.

- **The interface follows capability.**
  Use REST for operations REST supports and current GraphQL for everything REST cannot do, including reads and writes, without a one-off exception. Command specifications identify the REST capability gap; project operations use Projects V2, never deprecated Projects (classic) fields, types or mutations.

- **Delivery integrates each epic.**
  Task branches start from and their pull requests target the corresponding epic base, named `iNN/eNN/<long-lived-branch>`. Dependent tasks start after their prerequisites are delivered into that base.
- **Each epic reaches its long-lived targets.**
  A completed epic integrates each base into its corresponding configured long-lived branch after validation, current-head-and-base agent review and required human approval. An epic remains open until every base merges; other incomplete epics do not prevent its integration unless they are prerequisites.

- **Cross-epic starts follow available producer outputs.**
  A cross-epic consumer starts only when its named producer rows are delivered and their required outputs are verified available at the pinned consumer-base commit. Record the producer row, delivery evidence, output identity and consumer commit; a merge into a separate producer base alone is insufficient. Unrelated producer rows and producer-epic closure are not additional start gates. Whole-epic dependencies exist only where the task graph establishes the all-rows relationship. ## Overview

One skill holds the scheme. Its summary names every mode it offers, each mode is stated in a file of its own, and every shell operation a mode performs is a named command spec that mode cites. Work raised outside the structure reaches a place inside it, and an epic is created only once its tasks are whole.

## Problem

- **The scheme had no home.**
  The rules for initiatives, epics and tasks lived in the conversation that applied them, so each run restated them and no two runs restated them alike.
- **One file for every mode.**
  A single body loaded the whole scheme for a request that used one part of it, and a change to one mode's rules meant reading all of them to find where it belonged.
- **Operations written out at each site.**
  Each mode spelled out its own shell calls, so the same operation drifted between modes and a correction reached only the copy it was made in.
- **Work outside the structure.**
  An issue raised without a prefix belonged to no initiative, so it reached no board, no dependency check and no review.
- **Epics started on unfinished plans.**
  An epic could be created while a task had no work file, no tests and no Joins settled, and the gap surfaced only once the work began.

## Proposal

- **A mode per file.**
  The skill summary lists the modes and what each covers; the agent reads only the file for the mode the request calls for.
- **Command specs.**
  Every operation a mode performs is a named spec with its exact call, cited from the modes that use it, so one correction reaches every caller.
- **Shared authoring guidelines.**
  The guidelines that govern how a skill is written live in one file that each skill in the repository reads, rather than once per skill.
- **Hoist.**
  A mode places work raised outside the structure: into an existing task, a new task, a new epic or a new initiative, or it stays standalone. What a placed issue recorded is kept, in its new body or in a reference to it.
- **Readiness before creation.**
  Planning completes each task's work file, its tests and every eligible Joins pair before any issue of the epic exists.

content.body:
## Overview

An issue body reads the same whoever wrote it. Each item opens with a bold lead on its own line, states the design in at most two lines, links code from the words that carry it, and says what the system is rather than what changed. A Problem states the friction as it stands now, a pull request body states each functional change under its own lead, and a work file is prose rather than a table.

## Problem

- **Bodies that read as prose dumps.**
  An item ran to a paragraph with no lead, so a reader scanning for one facet read all of them.
- **A lead joined to its body.**
  A bold lead on the same line as its sentence left the two competing, and the lead stopped working as a label.
- **Links buried at the end.**
  A code reference sat after the sentence it supported rather than on the words that named it, so a reader followed the link to find out what it was for.
- **A Problem that described the plan.**
  Problems were written as what would be done, so nothing recorded the friction the work answers and a reviewer had no baseline.
- **Feedback answered in bulk.**
  A reply to review feedback restated the position rather than answering each point, so a reviewer could not tell which points were taken.
- **Work files as tables.**
  A task's own file repeated the epic's table instead of stating its design, so the detail a table cannot hold had nowhere to go.

## Proposal

- **Bold leads.**
  Each Problem and Proposal item opens with a bold lead, and the body sits on the line after it. A lead introducing sub-bullets keeps its introduction on the lead line.
- **Succinct items.**
  An item is at most two lines. Detail beyond that is a criterion of one invariant.
- **Links where the words are.**
  A code reference is linked from the words it supports, not appended to the item.
- **Present tense.**
  A Problem states the friction as it is now. No body carries the narrative of its own change.
- **Point by point.**
  A reply to issue feedback answers each point in turn, precisely and factually.
- **Pull request bodies.**
  Each functional change in a pull request body sits under its own bold lead.
- **Work files.**
  A task's file is paragraphs and bullets stating its design, not a table.

## Overview

An acceptance criterion states one invariant that something can fail. An initiative criterion ends by naming the instrument that keeps it; an epic criterion is a fact inspection, analysis, demonstration or test can check. Every row of a Work Breakdown names the criteria it delivers, every criterion is delivered by at least one row, and the criteria of an initiative agree with the sources it marks.

## Problem

- **Criteria nothing could fail.**
  A criterion worded as a judgement about meaning had no pass and no fail, so it was ticked on opinion.
- **Criteria with no instrument.**
  Nothing said how a criterion would be checked, so an initiative closed on a reading of its own text.
- **Detail hidden in table cells.**
  A row's Description carried the detail that should have been a criterion, so the work was specified in a place no review read as a specification.
- **Rows claiming no criterion.**
  A task could exist that delivered nothing the epic had stated, and a criterion could exist that no row delivered.
- **Sources that bound nothing.**
  An initiative could cite a requirements document in References while its criteria contradicted it, and no check compared the two.
- **No stated characteristics.**
  The qualities a requirement must have were applied from memory, so two reviews of one plan disagreed.

## Proposal

- **One invariant.**
  A criterion states a single condition that holds or does not. One joining several is split.
- **The instrument in the sentence.**
  An initiative criterion ends by naming what keeps it: an end-to-end walk, a smoke run, a live check, or a guard or fixture suite continuous integration runs. A named test that does not exist is work the plan holds.
- **Coverage.**
  Every row of a Work Breakdown names in Coverage the criteria it delivers, and a criterion no row delivers is a gap.
- **At least one.**
  A task covers at least one criterion, and a criterion more than one row cites is split into the invariant each row makes true.
- **Marked sources.**
  A reference the criteria answer to carries a mark. The criteria are then aligned with it in both directions: a criterion contradicting it is a fault, and a requirement it states that no criterion makes true and no Non-Goal excludes is a gap.
- **Stated characteristics.**
  The characteristics plan and review apply to a requirement are written down, and both modes read them.

content.body:
## Overview

Each theme has one project board, and every initiative of that theme stands on it with its epics and its task issues. An item's status follows from the state of its issue rather than from a judgement, an epic tracked in another repository still appears, and a board is brought current without a hand edit.

## Problem

- **One board for everything.**
  A single board held every initiative, so a view of one conversation's work meant filtering by hand and an initiative with no board was invisible.
- **Status set by hand.**
  Nothing derived an item's column from its issue, so a board drifted from the tracker as soon as anything moved.
- **Items missing from the board.**
  Epics and task issues existed that the board had never been told about, so a count taken from the board was wrong.
- **One repository assumed.**
  An epic tracked in another repository could not be held, so work spanning repositories had no board at all.
- **In Review assumed.**
  Every board was taken to have an In Review column, so a board without one could not be synchronised.

## Proposal

- **A board per theme.**
  Its title is the theme's name, a colon and its description. It is linked to the repository and holds that theme's initiatives, epics and task issues. A new theme needs its label and its board before an initiative takes it.
- **A derived status.**
  The column follows from facts already read: whether the issue is closed, whether its tasks are delivered, whether a pull request is open and whether it is a draft. A draft pull request leaves the item In Progress.
- **Missing items added.**
  An issue of the theme that the board does not hold is added to it.
- **Any repository.**
  An epic is tracked wherever its issue lives, and the board holds it.
- **In Review optional.**
  A board without an In Review column is synchronised to the columns it has.

## Overview

A board is read back as a standup. The summary opens with a paragraph a manager can read, lists each initiative with its epics and their tasks, names the few items that are next, and marks every item with one symbol for its state. A key explains the symbols, and the whole block pastes into Slack as written.

## Problem

- **Nothing to report from.**
  A board said where each item stood, but producing a status update from it meant reading every column and writing the account by hand each time.
- **No management line.**
  A summary of item states gave no account of what had been accomplished, so a reader outside the work could not tell what the period delivered.
- **Epics too coarse.**
  An epic line said an epic was in progress without saying which piece of work, so the summary did not answer what anyone was doing.
- **Every ready item listed.**
  Listing everything at Ready swamped the message, so the items that mattered next were lost in it.
- **Competing marks.**
  More than one symbol could stand for one state, so two summaries of the same board read differently and no key could explain either.
- **Slack formatting assumed.**
  Links were written in a form only a bot can post, so a summary pasted by a person showed its own markup.

- **A standup from the board.**
  One summary covers the whole board: each initiative, its epics, and each epic's tasks.
- **A paragraph for management.**
  The summary opens with a plain-language paragraph on what was accomplished, above the board line.
- **One mark per state.**
  Each state has exactly one symbol, each initiative is marked by its state, and the next task of an epic and each Next item carry the ready mark.
- **A short Next list.**
  Only the few highest-priority items at Ready appear under Next.
- **A key.**
  The summary closes with a key naming what each symbol and each letter stands for.
- **Pasteable links.**

## Overview

The plan follows what has landed. A task id links the pull requests on it, open or merged; a criterion ticks when it holds; a row ticks when it is delivered and its criteria are ticked; and an issue closes when its rows and criteria are complete. An initiative's work reaches a long-lived branch only once that initiative is whole.

## Problem

- **The plan went stale on delivery.**
  Work merged and nothing updated the issues, so the tracker described a state that had already passed.
- **No link from a row to its delivery.**
  A reader of a Work Breakdown could not tell which pull request delivered a row, or whether one was open on it.
- **A row ticked on sentiment.**
  Nothing tied a row's completion to its criteria, so a row could read as done while the conditions it covered were unmet.
- **No settled column for done.**
  Completion was recorded in different columns in different tables, so no check could read it.
- **Partial work on the trunk.**
  An initiative's pull requests merged to a long-lived branch as they passed, so a branch carried part of an initiative whose criteria were still open.
- **A mode named for its mechanism.**
  The mode that keeps the plan in step was named for updating, which described the call rather than the outcome.

## Proposal

- **Sync.**
  One mode brings the plan in step with what has landed, and is named for that.
- **Links from the row.**
  A task id links each pull request on it, open or merged, and a further pull request is linked after the ones already there.
- **Ticks that follow conditions.**
  A criterion ticks when it holds. A row ticks when it is delivered and every criterion its Coverage names is ticked. An epic closes when its criteria are ticked and its tasks delivered.
- **The last column.**
  Done is the last column of every Work Breakdown, empty while the row is open and a tick when it is complete.
- **Integration branches.**
  Each long-lived branch an initiative changes has an integration branch cut from it, and every pull request of that initiative targets it. The initiative stays open until each integration pull request has merged.

## Overview

A review reads a plan against itself. It reports an initiative criterion no epic covers and one ticked before the epics that cite it are delivered, a Work Breakdown cell that disagrees with what was delivered, and a criterion a merged pull request leaves unmet. Each finding names the issue and the cell it sits in, and the fix is made in the issue.

## Problem

- **Coverage checked one way.**
  A review could confirm an epic cited a criterion without confirming every criterion had an epic, so a criterion nothing delivered passed unnoticed.
- **Criteria ticked early.**
  An initiative criterion could be ticked while an epic citing it was still open, and nothing compared the tick against the epics.
- **Tables disagreeing with delivery.**
  A row could say delivered while its pull request was open, or say open while its pull request had merged, and the disagreement survived every review.
- **Unmet criteria lost on merge.**
  A pull request merged leaving a criterion of its task unmet, the task closed, and the criterion was never picked up again.

## Proposal

- **Coverage both ways.**
  Each initiative criterion is checked against every epic that cites it, and each epic is checked for the criteria it claims.
- **Ticks against the epics.**
  A criterion ticked while a citing epic is open is a finding, as is one unticked when every citing epic is complete.
- **Cells against delivery.**
  A Work Breakdown cell that disagrees with what its pull requests show is repaired to what was delivered.
- **A further task.**
  A criterion a merged pull request leaves unmet is adopted by a further task, which depends on the delivered one, and Done is held until it is.

## Overview

Work enters as a proposal. A mode states the problem, its evidence and its boundary, states the goal as clauses someone could observe, raises one issue carrying no number, and places it on a board of its own. Plan mode then takes that problem and goal as the scope it plans, and does not interview the scope again.

## Problem

- **Planning began with a solution.**
  A request became an initiative directly, so the friction and the evidence were never written down and every later review tested the plan against itself.
- **No place for work not yet taken up.**
  An idea had to become an initiative to be tracked at all, so the tracker held initiatives nobody had agreed to start.
- **Numbers spent too early.**
  An idea that might never run took an initiative number, and the numbering recorded intent rather than work.
- **No board for the funnel.**
  Nothing showed which proposals were being weighed, which were approved and which had been declined.

## Proposal

- **Propose mode.**
  It scopes the problem: the friction, the evidence and the boundary. It states the goal as clauses someone could observe. It raises one proposal issue, which carries no initiative number.
- **A board of its own.**
  The proposals board is copied from a template carrying its own statuses — Suggested, Considering, Approved, Held and Declined — and linked to the repository.
- **A handover to planning.**
  Plan mode takes a named proposal's Problem, Non-Goals and goal clauses as its scope, and every later review tests against those clauses.

content.body:
## Overview

A board hands out the work it makes available. Advance brings a theme board to the positions its issues imply and names what is ready, taking priority into account. Deliver runs Advance, then starts a session for each available unit of work, holding the row it has taken so no second run starts it elsewhere.

## Problem

- **Readiness decided by reading.**
  Finding what could start next meant reading every epic and its dependencies, so the answer varied with who read it.
- **Priority ignored.**
  Work was offered in issue order rather than by priority, so a board's most important available work was not the work offered first.
- **Nothing started the work.**
  A board could say what was ready without anything acting on it, so the step from a plan to a session was manual every time.
- **No hold on a row.**
  Nothing recorded that a session had taken a row, so two runs could start the same unit of work.
- **A hold with no release.**
  A session that died before opening a pull request would leave its row held, with nothing to notice or clear it.

## Proposal

- **Advance.**
  It brings the board's open initiatives in step, then names the available work by priority set.
- **Deliver.**
  It runs Advance, then dispatches a session for each available unit, which is one pull request's worth of work. The user confirms the set before anything starts.
- **The hold is a link.**
  A dispatched row links the planning folder its session will write. That link is the hold: a later run passes over a row that has one. The folder is named for the task's own issue, or for its epic's where the task has none.
- **Dispatched work moves.**
  A row a session has taken goes to In Progress.
- **A reported release.**
  Each run reports the rows held with no pull request open on them, and the user releases the ones whose session is gone.

content.body:
## Overview

A board reflects current delivery activity within initiative membership. Reservations and open pull requests keep work In Progress. Unstarted epics become Ready under a Ready or In Progress initiative when their prerequisites are met. Completed work retains Done, and epic In Review handoff requires agent review of the current integration diff. Sync reads every epic on the board, whatever table it carries.

## Problem

- **Historical delivery obscures current activity.**
  Completed work alone can keep an initiative In Progress even when it has no current delivery activity.
- **An epic outside the table counts.**
  An initiative is a candidate for In Progress on the strength of a completed epic its table does not list.
- **In Progress with no work under way.**
  One delivered row, or a pull request merged long ago, is enough to hold an epic In Progress, with nothing open on it.
- **Ready reached without the initiative.**
  An epic whose dependencies are delivered becomes Ready while its initiative sits in Backlog, so Ready fills with work nobody has started the initiative for.
- **Backlog leaves the epics behind.**
  Moving an initiative to Backlog leaves its epics where they were, still assigned.
- **Sync stops on an older table.**
  A closed epic carrying an earlier Work Breakdown has its tasks skipped, so its delivery is never read.
- **A linked pull request naming no epic.**
  A row links a merged pull request whose title carries no epic prefix, so the row is not seen as delivered and Done stays empty.
- **The branch set is read from a branch nobody delivers on.**
  The long-lived branches are read from the main working tree, which sits on the long-lived branch, so a statement an initiative changes is unreadable for that initiative's whole life and the epic checks gated on the set are passed over in silence.

## Proposal

- **Initiatives reflect their current members.**
  Current delivery activity in listed epics supports In Progress; completed work alone does not start another initiative. The board imposes no single-active-initiative limit.
- **Membership decides candidacy.**
  Only an epic still in the initiative's table counts towards that initiative being In Progress.
- **Reservations are active work.**
  An active task reservation or open delivery pull request makes its epic In Progress until completion and reviewed-handoff conditions are met. A persistent epic integration draft alone is not task activity.
- **Review gates the handoff.**
  An epic becomes In Review only after completion checks and recorded agent review of the current integration head and base pass, with no unresolved blocking finding. Missing or stale review keeps a completed, unmerged epic In Progress; human approval still governs merge.
- **Ready opens on the initiative.**
  An unstarted epic is eligible for Ready while its initiative is Ready or In Progress, its dependencies are delivered and its planning prerequisites are met. An unresolved prerequisite keeps unstarted work in Backlog.
  An initiative awaiting its priority decision, or kept In Progress only while its open pull requests finish, readies none of its epics.
- **Backlog takes the tree.**
  An initiative in Backlog holds its unstarted epics and task issues in Backlog, with no assignee. Completed descendants retain Done; active reservations, open delivery pull requests and review handoffs require explicit reconciliation before a parent can be parked, rather than automatic release or reassignment.
- **Every epic read.**
  A closed epic is brought to the current Work Breakdown columns before sync reads its tasks.
- **The link names its epic.**
  Sync retitles a merged pull request a row links so its title starts with that row's epic prefix.
- **The theme is named.**
  The skill's themes table names the planning theme and its board, as it does the others.
- **The project states its own branches.**
  A project names its long-lived branches in `config/branches` at the evaluated commit. The run records the repository, resolved commit and configuration path; invocation worktree and uncommitted edits do not choose the source.
- **The reading reaches the branch under delivery.**
  An epic sync evaluates its pinned epic-base commit; verification of merged delivery evaluates that merged commit. An absent, empty or unreadable declaration is unevaluable and names the affected checks; no other revision, working tree or branch-name inference supplies a fallback.
- **Every long-lived branch carries the declaration.**
  `main`, `workflows` and `docker` each commit `config/branches` naming the set `workspace` names, so an epic base cut from any of them reads its own declaration.
- **A unit reaches every base it changes.**
  A unit that changes several long-lived branches has one task branch and worktree per epic base, named for its long-lived branch, and its row links every pull request it delivers through.
- **Delivery reaches only what a unit changes.**
  A unit is given branches only for the bases it changes, every Record Epic Delivery caller passes the epic's bases, and sync checks a link's prefix in the run that makes it.
- **The queue parks an idle epic as the board does.**
  An inactive epic In Progress under a waiting initiative returns to Backlog in the queue, as the board delivery returns it, and the cascade test asserts the call it means.

## Overview

The scheme's rules divide into those a script decides and those a reader is trusted to remember. This epic moves the second group into the first: the conventions binding the skill's own files, and the delivery conventions binding the pull requests that carry initiative work, each reach a named operation the fixture suite runs.

## Problem

- **The skill's own files are checked by memory.**
  The frontmatter's trigger phrases, the one-line prose layout, the single vocabulary and the split between the shared guide and the skill's own are stated as rules and enforced by whoever notices a departure. Only the mode summary has a check.
- **A command can be spelled out twice.**
  The rule that every command is specified once and reached by its operation name has no check, so a mode file that inlines a call reads as correct.
- **The interface rule has no guard.**
  The interface check must distinguish supported REST operations, capabilities requiring current GraphQL, and deprecated Projects (classic) APIs; a blanket non-REST rejection blocks required reads and writes.
- **Delivery conventions go unreported.**
  A renumbering that moves an identifier delivered work carries, an initiative pull request whose title names no epic, and a task pull request targeting anything other than its corresponding epic base are each caught, when they are caught, by review.
- **A record file is named twice.**
  The work item's name is composed once by the session writing the record's README and once by the operation writing the epic row's link, and nothing reads one against the other, so a row can link a file the record does not hold.

## Proposal

- **One check per rule, reached by name.**
  Each rule gets an operation in its owning artifact and a check in the fixture suite, so a mode file names the operation and the suite decides the rule.
- **The skill's files are an input like any other.**
  The checks over the skill read its frontmatter, its mode files, its references and its scripts the way the format check reads an issue body.
- **The delivery checks extend what already reads pull requests.**
  The title and base conventions are decided where the sync already parses an initiative's pull requests, and the renumber refusal extends the one the renumber script already makes for linked work.
- **A file carries one composition.**
  The work item's name is composed the one way, and the operation that writes the row's link refuses a name the record does not hold.

- **The interface follows capability.**
  Use REST where it supports the operation and current GraphQL for everything REST cannot do, without a one-off exception. Command specifications state the REST capability gap; project operations use Projects V2, never deprecated Projects (classic) fields, types or mutations.

- **Delivery integrates each epic.**
  Task branches start from and their pull requests target the corresponding epic base, named `iNN/eNN/<long-lived-branch>`. Dependent tasks start after their prerequisites are delivered into that base.
- **Each epic reaches its long-lived targets.**
  A completed epic integrates each base into its corresponding configured long-lived branch after validation, current-head-and-base agent review and required human approval. An epic remains open until every base merges; other incomplete epics do not prevent its integration unless they are prerequisites.

- **Final conformance uses settled inputs.**
  The whole-repository verification runs after the epic's remaining checker, instruction and cleanup changes land. It runs the shared check by hand over every skill in I11's scope, naming each, with no accepted-failure baseline, and records the tested revision; later input changes require a fresh pass.

- **Execution callers and retrieval reach are distinct.**
  Only a procedure that runs an operation counts as its caller. Required citations, including those inside command specifications, contribute to retrieval evidence without increasing caller counts. Placement follows the declared mode, protocol and artifact structure; artifact commands stay with their owning subject.
- **Retrieval measurements feed the final comparison.**
  This epic produces identified read traces and measurements. Binding Citations owns the final no-increase verdict after the contributing layout edits and final manifests are complete.

- **Cross-epic starts follow available producer outputs.**
  A cross-epic consumer starts only when its named producer rows are delivered and their required outputs are verified available at the pinned consumer-base commit. Record the producer row, delivery evidence, output identity and consumer commit; a merge into a separate producer base alone is insufficient. Unrelated producer rows and producer-epic closure are not additional start gates. Whole-epic dependencies exist only where the task graph establishes the all-rows relationship. Existing integration, review and human-approval requirements still apply.

- **A command acting on its checkout names which one.**
  A closed vocabulary of checkouts stands in the entry point's Conventions. A command whose behaviour depends on its working directory declares so, each procedure declares the checkout it runs in, and each call site names one from the vocabulary.

## Overview

This epic makes every run read what the plan records. The test plan is the merge gate and the one table of Test, Description, Coverage and Pass, the Work Breakdown is the dependency graph, and nothing yet reads the marks the plan holds, repairs a plan written to an earlier shape, tells an unreadable plan from an untested criterion, reads a row whose Task cell carries more than one link, or tells a dependency entry it cannot read from a prerequisite that has not landed.

## Problem

- **Nothing reads the Pass marks.**
  `plan_claims` in `sync.py` destructures the Pass cell and discards it, feeding only the disagreement report. A merged pull request leaves its epic's criteria unticked, and the evidence that would settle each one sits in the pull request unread.
- **An alignment brings no plan current.**
  The step that repaired a pull request's test plan went with the two-structure mismatch it policed, and nothing replaced it. A pull request carrying the retired checked list and `Test | Criteria` table is never brought to the shape the skill states.
- **The gap is silent and it accumulates.**
  Twelve merged pull requests on one private initiative carried the retired shape. No check reported them, and each was converted by hand.
- **An unreadable plan reads as an untested criterion.**
  A plan no parser can read yields no claims, which reports as a criterion nothing tested, so the message names the wrong cause and the repair it implies is the wrong repair.
- **A reference may carry a private URL into a public ticket.**
  A References section copied from a private repository's planning record reaches a ticket anyone can read.
- **A doubly linked row leaves the dependency graph.** A unit spanning two trees links a pull request per tree, so its Task cell repeats its id. [The row filter](https://github.com/m2ux/workflow-server/blob/360f0081/skills/work-planner/scripts/deps.py#L66-L68) in `deps.py` matches the whole cell against one id and skips the row, which then contributes no node and no edge:
  - every dependency and Joins entry naming it is reported unknown;
  - the levels, the longest chains and the whole-epic report are computed over a table with holes in it;
  - a run over I04's fourteen epics reported eight such problems across six epics, each naming a row that exists and is delivered.
- **A malformed task id passes unnamed.**
  A Task cell carrying an extra digit resolves to the row its first three characters spell, and one carrying too few is skipped, so a typo in the column that holds a row's identity becomes the wrong row or no row at all.
- **An unreadable dependency entry is a hard problem to one tool and an unmet prerequisite to the other.**
  `deps.py` [names it and exits nonzero](https://github.com/m2ux/workflow-server/blob/267d4c4e68d453686107825e7a8f449efb9eae42/skills/work-planner/scripts/deps.py#L121), while [`met` in `board.py`](https://github.com/m2ux/workflow-server/blob/267d4c4e68d453686107825e7a8f449efb9eae42/skills/work-planner/scripts/board.py#L220-L223) appends `links no issue` to `unresolved` and returns `False`, the answer it gives a prerequisite that has not landed. The two are indistinguishable downstream, so a planner who runs only the queue sees a row that stays blocked and no statement of why.
- **A permanent condition is modelled as a temporary one.**
  An entry naming an issue that does not exist, a row its epic does not carry, or nothing parseable at all can never become satisfied, and `False` says only that it is not satisfied yet. Twenty-three of twenty-three cross-epic cells on one private initiative were unreadable for the length of four epics, with the queue placing rows throughout.
- **The joins advisory invites the assertion it is meant to prevent.**
  The [advisory](https://github.com/m2ux/workflow-server/blob/267d4c4e68d453686107825e7a8f449efb9eae42/skills/work-planner/scripts/deps.py#L180) names every independent pair, and the cheapest way to silence it is to name the pair in Joins, asserting a pull request they will never share, as two epics of that initiative did, one with thirteen rows each naming the other twelve. The planning-record entry that properly resolves the line silences nothing, and nothing checks that it exists.

## Proposal

- **A passed check ticks the criterion it observes.**
  Sync Epic reads the Pass cell of each linked pull request's test plan and ticks the epic criteria those passed checks name.
- **Alignment repairs a plan written to an earlier shape.**
  Align mode converts a retired checked list and `Test | Criteria` table into the one table, and reports each pull request it converted.
- **An unreadable plan is diagnosed as unreadable.**
  A plan that yields no claims is reported as a plan nothing can read, distinct from a criterion no test observes.
- **A reference is checked against the repository that will hold it.**
  A References entry citing a private repository is a finding when the issue is public.
- **A row is read by the id at the head of its Task cell.**
  The repeated-id form, the single-link form and the bare id all name one row. A cell whose links disagree on the id is a defect in the table, reported rather than skipped.
- **A task id is a W and two digits.**
  Every id a Task cell carries is held to that form, and one that departs from it is reported with the epic and the id as written.
- **A dependency entry that cannot resolve is its own outcome.**
  `met` returns unresolvable for an unparseable entry, an issue it was not given and a row an epic does not carry, distinct from the answer a prerequisite that has not landed receives.
- **One field carries one verdict across the tools that read it.**
  Whatever severity the dependency check assigns an unreadable entry, the board queue assigns the same: it names the row and the entry and leaves the row unplaced rather than reporting it as waiting.
- **The advisory names both resolutions, and the record is held to the one it claims.**
  The printed line states that an independent pair either shares a pull request and names it in Joins or is accounted for in the planning record, and a pair in neither is reported.

| [W03](https://github.com/m2ux/workflow-server/pull/1266) | Dependency rows read by task id | AC5, AC6, AC7 | | | ✓ |

| [W06](https://github.com/m2ux/workflow-server/pull/1467) | Joins advisory names both resolutions | AC11, AC12 | | W05 | ✓ |

## Acceptance Criteria

- [x] **AC1.** Sync Epic ticks an epic criterion when a linked pull request's test plan carries a passed check naming it, as the skill's fixture suite shows against a plan with and without the tick.
- [x] **AC2.** Align mode converts a pull request carrying the retired checked list and `Test | Criteria` table into the one table, and names each pull request it converted, as the skill's fixture suite shows.
- [x] **AC3.** A test plan no parser can read is reported as unreadable rather than as a criterion no test observes, as the skill's fixture suite shows against a malformed plan.
- [x] **AC4.** A References entry citing a private repository is reported when the issue is public, as the skill's fixture suite shows.
- [x] **AC5.** A Work Breakdown row whose Task cell links the same task id more than once is read as that row, as the skill's fixture suite shows against a table carrying the repeated-id, single-link and bare-id spellings.
- [x] **AC6.** A Task cell whose links name different ids is reported as a problem, as the skill's fixture suite shows against a table carrying one.
- [x] **AC7.** The dependency check reports no unknown dependency and no unknown Joins entry naming a row the table carries, as a run over the repository's open epics shows.
- [x] **AC8.** A Task cell naming a task id that is not a W and two digits is reported with the id as written, as the skill's fixture suite shows against a table carrying one in the head position and one after it.
- [x] **AC9.** A `Depends on` entry that cannot resolve is reported as unresolvable by the board queue and by the dependency check alike, as the skill's fixture suite shows against a plan carrying an unparseable entry, an issue that is not given and a row its epic does not carry.
- [x] **AC10.** A board queue run meeting an unresolvable `Depends on` entry names the row and the entry and leaves the row unplaced, as the skill's fixture suite shows against a plan carrying one.
- [x] **AC11.** The joins advisory names the Joins cell and the planning-record entry as the two resolutions open to a planner, as the skill's fixture suite shows against an epic carrying an independent pair.
- [x] **AC12.** An independent pair of tasks named in neither its epic's Joins nor the planning record is reported, as the skill's fixture suite shows against a plan carrying an unrecorded pair.

## Overview

Work Planner states 79 command specifications in one catalog, and every mode opens that catalog to reach the few operations its procedure runs. This epic puts each specification in the file whose procedure runs it, leaves the catalog holding only what several procedures share, fixes the set of top-level sections a mode file may carry across both skills, moves Workflow Canon's specifications the same way, and reaches both rules through the shared skill-file check so the layout holds without anyone remembering it.

## Problem

- **One catalog answers every mode.**
  [`references/commands.md`](https://github.com/m2ux/workflow-server/blob/fae97e9e/skills/work-planner/references/commands.md) holds 79 specifications across 870 lines, 30 percent of the skill's markdown, and all ten mode files link into it. 36 of the 79 are cited from one file.
- **The conventions ride on the catalog.**
  The execution conventions every specification assumes sit at the head of that file, so a procedure reaching them opens the file holding all 79.
- **A mode file may invent a top-level section.**
  [`skills/guidelines.md`](https://github.com/m2ux/workflow-server/blob/fae97e9e/skills/guidelines.md#L51) states that a section the procedure draws on sits beside it under a heading of its own, so nothing fixes what a mode file carries. Eight such sections stand: Brief and Placements in Work Planner, and Canon Question, Attribution, Coverage, Branch Coverage, Findings and Verdicts in Workflow Canon. What a mode states, and where, is not predictable from the file before it.
- **The specification rule reports three results it should not.**
  [`check_skill_files.py`](https://github.com/m2ux/workflow-server/blob/9ed47b0d/skills/scripts/check_skill_files.py#L148) counts a specification's callers without the file that holds it, so one its own procedure cites alongside a single other file is reported. [Inside a catalog](https://github.com/m2ux/workflow-server/blob/9ed47b0d/skills/scripts/check_skill_files.py#L110) every third-level heading counts as a specification, so `### Execution` under `## Conventions` is one. A [caller under another root](https://github.com/m2ux/workflow-server/blob/9ed47b0d/skills/scripts/check_skill_files.py#L150) raises `ValueError` rather than drawing a finding.
- **Any citation from the holding file excludes a specification.**
  [`check_skill_files.py`](https://github.com/m2ux/workflow-server/blob/67fe12ad/skills/scripts/check_skill_files.py#L162) counts the file holding a specification among its callers whatever cites it there, and a catalog holds no procedure, so eleven specifications in [`commands.md`](https://github.com/m2ux/workflow-server/blob/67fe12ad/skills/work-planner/references/commands.md) are excluded by a sibling specification's cross-reference rather than by the procedure that runs them.
- **The section rule reads only the headings present.**
  [`skills/guidelines.md`](https://github.com/m2ux/workflow-server/blob/9ed47b0d/skills/guidelines.md#L50) makes Procedure and Rules mandatory, and the check measures membership and order alone, so a mode file carrying neither passes.
- **Five links resolve by file order.**
  [`review-criteria.md`](https://github.com/m2ux/workflow-server/blob/fae97e9e/skills/work-planner/references/review-criteria.md) titles a heading `Proposal` four times and `Acceptance Criteria` three times, once per issue kind. Five of those repeats are cited, and each citation reaches the first heading of that title rather than the kind it names.
- **Two layout faults stand against the shared check.**
  [`hoist-mode.md:81`](https://github.com/m2ux/workflow-server/blob/fae97e9e/skills/work-planner/references/hoist-mode.md#L81) carries a 113-character inline bold lead against a 100-character limit, and [`standup-mode.md`](https://github.com/m2ux/workflow-server/blob/fae97e9e/skills/work-planner/references/standup-mode.md#L57) ends on a blank line.

## Proposal

- **A specification stands in the file whose procedure runs it.**
  Each mode file gains a Commands section holding the operations only that mode runs, with the conventions governing them stated in the entry point every mode opens. The reader meets the operation at the point of use rather than through a link out.
- **The catalog keeps what several procedures share.**
  Specifications cited from more than one file stay in one place, so an operation two modes run is still stated once and changed once.
- **The conventions stand in the entry point.**
  Work Planner's execution conventions are a section of `SKILL.md`, which every mode opens to select itself, so a procedure reaching them opens no further file and the statement stands once.
- **A mode file carries five top-level sections.**
  Prerequisites, Procedure, Reference, Rules and Commands, in that order, each optional but for Procedure and Rules. Anything else a mode needs is a sub-section under one of them, so a diverse title names a part of a known whole rather than a section a reader must discover.
- **What the reader does with a heading places it.**
  Reference holds what a step consults or produces — a table, an output shape, a vocabulary. Rules holds what binds the mode whatever step it is on. An alternative way into the mode is a step of the Procedure. The test is stated once in the shared guidelines, so the next author places a heading without a precedent to copy.
- **One check decides both rules.**
  `skills/scripts/check_skill_files.py` gains a rule for a specification cited from one file other than its own, and a rule for a top-level section outside the named set or out of its order. Both bind every skill in the repository, so the layout is measured rather than remembered.
- **A specification's callers include the file that holds it.**
  The count reads every citation, so a specification already standing in the procedure that runs it draws no finding whatever else cites it, and a caller under another root is reported rather than raised.
- **A step is what calls a command.**
  A passage runs the commands it names where its author has written them as steps, and a sentence naming commands names them. Mood, count, order and condition each divide one pair of passages and join another, so enumeration is the only mark an author, a reader and the check all read alike.
- **A procedure's citation is what makes a file a caller.**
  One reading settles every file: a file is a caller where one of its procedures runs the command, whether or not it holds the specification, so a cross-reference between two specifications counts for neither and a procedure stated under its own heading counts wherever it stands.
- **Each rule reads the whole of what the guidelines state.**
  A command specification is a heading the Commands listing carries, not every third-level heading in the file, and a mandatory section is reported by its absence as well as by its place.
- **The reduction is measured.**
  Each mode's retrieval is recorded under the skill's representative scenarios against the layout before the change and the layout after it, so the claim rests on a walk rather than on arithmetic.

## Work Breakdown

| [W17](https://github.com/m2ux/workflow-server/pull/1401) | Catalog listings named for what runs them | AC20 | W08 | | ✓ |

## Acceptance Criteria

- [x] **AC1.** The shared skill-file check reports a command specification cited from exactly one file other than the one holding it, as the check's own test suite shows against a specimen skill carrying that fault.
- [x] **AC2.** The shared skill-file check reports a mode file carrying a top-level section outside the set the shared guidelines name, or carrying those sections out of the order they name, as the check's own test suite shows against a specimen skill carrying each fault.

- [x] **AC4.** Every link in the skill's files resolves to one file and one heading, as the shared skill-file check reports over the skill's files.
- [x] **AC5.** Each of the skill's mode files carries only the top-level sections the shared guidelines name, in the order they name them, as the shared skill-file check reports over the skill's files.

- [x] **AC7.** Each of the Workflow Canon skill's mode files carries only the top-level sections the shared guidelines name, in the order they name them, as the shared skill-file check reports over that skill's files.
- [x] **AC8.** The shared skill-file check reports no command-specification finding for a specification the procedure holding it cites, as the check's own test suite shows against a specimen carrying that citation and one other.
- [x] **AC9.** The shared skill-file check reads a command specification as a heading the Commands listing carries, as the check's own test suite shows against a specimen catalog whose conventions section carries a cited heading.
- [x] **AC10.** The shared skill-file check reports a citation whose caller lies under another of the roots it is given, as the check's own test suite shows against two specimen skills with different parents.

- [x] **AC12.** The shared skill-file check counts the file holding a command specification among its callers only where a procedure of that file cites it, as the check's own test suite shows against a specimen catalog whose sibling specification carries the citation.

- [x] **AC15.** A passage runs the commands it names where its author has written them as steps, as the shared guidelines state and the check's own test suite shows against a specimen carrying a prose route and one carrying the same commands as steps.

## Overview

Work Planner is a general-purpose skill, and one rule in it holds for this project alone: an epic whose tasks change workflow definitions must carry a corpus audit criterion. This epic gives the skill a general statement that a project may require criteria of its epics, a declaration the project fills in, and moves the corpus audit into this project's declaration, so the guide states the mechanism and the project states its own answer.

## Problem

- **One project's doctrine is stated as the skill's law.**
  The Corpus Audit section of the Work Breakdown Guide fixes the criterion's wording, the row's name and the audit that evidences it. A project with no definition corpus meets a rule it cannot satisfy and cannot switch off.
- **The engine matches this project's vocabulary.**
  `format.py` decides an epic's compliance by searching its criteria for the phrase `canon audit`. A general-purpose check tests for a term only this project uses.
- **The parameterisation stops at the branch.**
  `Check Format` takes `--corpus`, so the branch the corpus lives on is a project value. The meaning attached to that branch is not, which made the rule read as general when it is not.
- **The skill already has the seam this rule should have used.**
  A project states its long-lived branches in `config/branches` at its root. The guide states the rule, reports the names unevaluable when the file is absent, and names this project's values only under a labelled Example.

## Proposal

- **A project declares the criteria its epics must carry.**
  The guide states that a project may require a criterion of an epic whose rows reach a named branch, and where the project declares it. Which criterion, and on which branch, is the project's to state.
- **A declared criterion carries what the check needs to report it.**
  The condition that triggers it, the criterion's text, a phrase identifying it in an epic that already carries it, and the name of the row that delivers it.
- **An absent declaration is unevaluable, never defaulted.**
  A project declaring nothing neither acquires this project's corpus audit nor silently loses a requirement it meant to state, which is how `config/branches` already reports a missing statement.
- **The corpus audit becomes this project's declaration.**
  Its substance is unchanged and this repository's epics carry it exactly as they do now. What changes is where it is stated, and that `format.py` carries no vocabulary of its own.

- **The evaluated revision owns the declaration.**
  Resolve the subject revision to a commit and read required-criteria configuration there, recording repository, commit and path. Epic checks use the epic-base commit; merged-delivery verification uses the merged commit. Invocation worktrees and uncommitted edits do not supply configuration. Missing, empty or unreadable declarations are explicitly unevaluable, with no fallback to another revision or project defaults.
- **A declared criterion states what brings it.**
  An entry names the paths whose change brings its criterion, so work reaching the branch without touching them carries none. The criterion's text states what leaves a finding outstanding.

## Work Breakdown

| Task | Description | Coverage | Depends on | Joins | Done |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [W01](https://github.com/m2ux/workflow-server/pull/1504) | A project declares the criteria its epics carry | AC1 | | | ✓ |

content.body:
## Overview

Delivery keeps the board and the review pull request in step with what has landed. A task's criteria are readable from the evidence its open pull request carries, a row a session holds reads as work in progress, a completed epic's review pull request stands for review, and every board write a delivery run makes is one that run owns.

## Problem

- **A task's criteria are unreadable until its work has merged.**
  They are reported ready to verify only once the delivering pull request has merged, though the evidence they rest on is what that pull request and its planning record already carry.
- **A held row reads as Ready.**
  A row a session holds derives no status from its reservation, so a sync returns its issue to Ready after a dispatch set it In Progress.
- **A complete epic waits on a click.**
  Its review pull request stays a draft until the user marks it ready, though every condition for that mark is one the delivery scripts already establish, and the merge still belongs to the reviewer where the target requires a review.
- **A delivery run writes the board unchecked.**
  Board writes go through one component that refuses a status the calling mode does not own, and a delivery run's writes are the only ones that bypass it.

## Proposal

- **A task's evidence is its pull request, not its merge.**
  Its criteria are reported ready to verify once a pull request names the task, open or merged. Delivery and closure still wait on the merge.
- **A held row reads as In Progress.**
  A row whose id links its planning record derives that status, so a sync agrees with the dispatch that set it.
- **The signal that completes an epic readies its draft.**
  The sync reports a base unmerged once every task is delivered and every criterion ticked, naming the pull request that merges it. A draft named there is taken out of draft, and the epic moves to In Review. The mark states completion, not permission: the epic merge conditions decide the merge.
- **A delivery run's board writes are held to a jurisdiction.**
  It owns the In Progress a held row and its epic take and the In Review a completed epic takes. Any other status, a task set In Review, and a removal are refused.

## Overview

Three reads the skill names have no command behind them: the Development relation read from each end, a closure condition no single-issue gate can see, and a checkout at the revision a criterion is verified against. This epic supplies them as commands the artifact operations name, so a sync run spends one call per subject rather than assembling evidence by hand.

## Problem

Each required read costs one call per subject or none at all, so a run either spends them or approximates the result.

- **The link snapshot is specified and unreadable at scale.**
  Fetching pull-request issue links runs the Development read once for every pull request in the collection. One initiative held 113, so the snapshot cost 113 calls and nothing checked that it was complete.

- **The same field, read from the issue end, is named but never run.**
  The issue read says to sweep every page and state without naming a command, so the skill has no command block for either end of the relation.

- **A literal dollar sign cannot reach the tracker through this shell.**
  A GraphQL variable is a `$`, which the workspace denies, so the relation is only readable through a query file passed with `-F query=@file`. Composing that file for 113 aliases by hand is where a repository or a page is quietly lost.

- **Nothing reports a closure its own evidence does not support.**
  The closure gate decides one issue against fresh evidence. No command answers the repository-wide question, so an issue closed as completed with criteria unticked is found by reading, or not at all.

- **A criterion is verified in a checkout a run must build and then remembers to remove.**
  The instrument checkout requires the merged revision and states that an edited checkout is not it. A sync run created three detached worktrees by hand, and the project now carries six it never removed.

## Proposal

- **Two scripts read the relation, one from each end.**
  The issue-end read sweeps every issue's Development field in batches, and the pull-request-end read writes the link array the epic sync consumes. Each takes the paginated REST collection the skill already tells a caller to fetch.

- **The query is generated into a file, never inlined.**
  The script writes the aliased GraphQL document and passes it with `-F query=@file`, so no command carries the character the shell denies and no alias is composed by hand.

- **An unread field is missing evidence, not an empty link set.**
  A relation the tracker could not read is printed and the run exits nonzero, matching the skill's rule that incomplete evidence is a blocker rather than a partial result.

- **A sweep reports the closure condition the single-issue gate cannot see.**
  Closed issues whose criteria are unticked or whose Development-linked pull request has not merged are listed with the issue's state reason.

- **A revision is materialized, used, and removed in one call.**
  The helper resolves the supplied reference to a commit, creates a detached checkout at it, runs the named instrument there, and removes the checkout whatever the instrument returns.

- **The skill keeps the specification and the scripts stay beside it.**
  Each script is a command block in the artifact operation that names it, with a test under the skill's test directory and a structure declaration.

- **Capture uses the supported interface for each capability.**
  Use REST where it exposes the required data and current GraphQL for capabilities REST cannot provide, without a one-off exception. Development relation reads use the current issue and pull-request schema; any project operation uses Projects V2 and never deprecated Projects (classic) fields, types or mutations.

- **Dependencies follow consumed evidence.**
  The closure sweep consumes complete Development captures and their missing-evidence behavior. The revision helper consumes a repository revision and command, independently of capture. A final reachability audit checks all delivered scripts; each implementation supplies its own command specification, caller wiring and tests.

- **Development links are written by command.**
  The add and remove mutations run as `gh api graphql` calls from a query file and are read back from both ends, so a missing browser or connector is never reported as an unavailable field.

## Overview

Require an agent review of an epic's complete integration diff before its In Review handoff to the user. The handoff should include a recorded review of the current integration head and base and the disposition of every finding.

## Problem

- **Delivery checks do not establish review completion.**
